idea: Rust is installed and managed with **rustup**, the official toolchain installer. One command installs three things: `rustc`, the compiler that turns `.rs` source files into native programs; `cargo`, the build tool and package manager you will use every day; and the standard library with its documentation. rustup also keeps several **toolchains** side by side (stable, beta, nightly, or a pinned version for one project) and updates them with `rustup update`.

Rust releases a new stable version every six weeks. Updates are backwards compatible: code that compiled last year still compiles. Larger language changes are grouped into **editions** (2015, 2018, 2021, 2024) that each crate opts into in its `Cargo.toml`, so the language can evolve without breaking old code. New projects use the latest edition.

Two more pieces complete the setup. **rust-analyzer**, the language server, gives your editor completion, inline types and instant errors; install it as your editor's Rust extension. And `rustup doc` opens the standard library documentation and the Rust Book **offline**, which is handy when you are on a train or the website is slow.

Update: `rustup update`; pin a project with a `rust-toolchain.toml` file.
Add tools: `rustup component add clippy rustfmt`.
Offline docs: `rustup doc` (or `rustup doc --book`, `rustup doc --std`).
Editor: install the rust-analyzer extension.

idea: Every Rust program starts at a function called `main`. `fn main() { ... }` declares it: `fn` introduces a function, the parentheses hold parameters (none here), and the body sits in curly braces. Inside, `println!("Hello, world!");` prints a line. The `!` means `println!` is a **macro**, not a function: macros generate code at compile time, which lets `println!` check its format string and arguments before the program ever runs. Statements end with a semicolon.

Rust is a **compiled** language. `rustc main.rs` reads the source, checks it thoroughly (types, ownership, borrowing) and produces a native executable, `main` (or `main.exe` on Windows), that runs without Rust installed. Compiling and running are separate steps: you can give the executable to someone else and they run it directly. The compiler's checks are strict, and its error messages are famously helpful: they point at the exact spot, explain the problem and often suggest the fix.

Formatting with `println!` uses placeholders: `{}` for a value's user-facing form, `{:?}` for its debug form, and you can put variable names directly inside the braces: `println!("{name} is {age}")`. Code style is standardised by `rustfmt`: four spaces of indentation and braces on the same line.

idea: Real projects use **Cargo**, Rust's build system and package manager. `cargo new hello_cargo` creates a folder with a `Cargo.toml` manifest (the package's name, version, edition and dependencies), a `src/main.rs` with a hello-world program, and a fresh git repository with a `.gitignore`. From then on, Cargo builds the right files with the right flags, and downloads and compiles any **crates** (libraries) you depend on.

Four commands cover daily work. `cargo build` compiles into `target/debug/`. `cargo run` builds if needed and runs the program. `cargo check` only checks that the code compiles, without producing an executable, which is much faster and ideal while writing code. `cargo build --release` compiles with optimisations into `target/release/`; it takes longer to build but the program runs much faster, so it is what you measure and ship.

Cargo also creates `Cargo.lock`, which records the exact versions of every dependency, so builds are reproducible. The `target/` folder holds build output and is ignored by git. Other everyday commands: `cargo fmt` formats the code, `cargo clippy` runs the linter, `cargo test` runs tests and `cargo doc --open` builds documentation for your project and its dependencies.

idea: The guessing game starts by reading what the player types. Input comes from **standard input**, reached through `std::io::stdin()`. Its `read_line` method appends the typed line, including the newline, to a `String` you provide. That string must be **mutable** (`let mut guess = String::new();`), because variables in Rust are immutable by default and `read_line` needs to change it.

The string is passed as `&mut guess`: a **mutable reference**. `read_line` borrows the string to write into it, without taking ownership, so you can still use `guess` afterwards. The `&mut` makes it explicit at the call site that the function will modify your variable, a theme you will see throughout Rust.

Reading can fail (the input might not be valid UTF-8, or the stream might be closed), so `read_line` returns a **`Result`**: either `Ok` with the number of bytes read, or `Err` with an error. Rust will not let you silently ignore it; the compiler warns about an unused `Result`. For now, `.expect("Failed to read line")` says "crash with this message if it failed"; later lessons handle errors gracefully. `use std::io;` at the top brings the module into scope so you can write `io::stdin()`.
how: `use std::io;` then `let mut guess = String::new();`.
`io::stdin().read_line(&mut guess).expect("Failed to read line");`
`read_line` appends, including the newline; `guess.trim()` removes it.
Returns `Result<usize>`: the byte count on success.

idea: The standard library has no random-number generator, so the game uses a **crate**: a package of Rust code published on crates.io. Adding one is a single line in the `[dependencies]` section of `Cargo.toml` (`rand = "0.9"`), or `cargo add rand`. The next build downloads it and everything it depends on, compiles them, and links them in.

The version requirement `"0.9"` is a **semantic versioning** range: any version compatible with 0.9 (0.9.0 up to, but not including, 0.10.0). On the first build, Cargo picks the newest matching versions and writes them to **`Cargo.lock`**. Later builds, on any machine, use exactly those versions until you run `cargo update`, which is what makes builds reproducible: a new release of a crate never changes your program by surprise.

To use the crate, bring what you need into scope and call it: `rand::random_range(1..=100)` returns a random integer from 1 to 100 inclusive (`..=` is an inclusive range; `1..100` would stop at 99). Each crate's documentation is on docs.rs, and `cargo doc --open` builds the docs for exactly the versions in your lock file.
how: `cargo add rand` or add `rand = "0.9"` under `[dependencies]`.

idea: To compare the guess with the secret, the text must become a number. `guess.trim().parse::<u32>()` (or `let guess: u32 = guess.trim().parse()...`) converts it, and returns a `Result`, because "abc" is not a number. The type annotation tells `parse` what to produce; Rust infers types almost everywhere, but here there is nothing else to infer from.

`guess.cmp(&secret)` compares two values and returns an `Ordering`, an enum with three variants: `Less`, `Greater` and `Equal`. A **`match`** expression handles each one in its own **arm**, and the compiler checks that every variant is covered, so you cannot forget a case.

The game repeats with **`loop`**, an infinite loop that you leave with **`break`** when the guess is right. Bad input should not crash the game: instead of `expect`, match on the `Result` from `parse`. `Ok(num) => num` uses the number; `Err(_) => continue` skips to the next round (the underscore is a catch-all that ignores the error's details). This shift, from crashing on errors to handling them, is the heart of idiomatic Rust.
how: `let guess: u32 = match guess.trim().parse() { Ok(n) => n, Err(_) => continue };`
`use std::cmp::Ordering;` then `match guess.cmp(&secret) { Ordering::Less => ..., ... }`.
`loop { ... }` repeats; `break` leaves; `continue` starts the next pass.

idea: In Rust, variables are **immutable by default**: `let x = 5;` binds a value that cannot change. Trying to assign `x = 6;` is a compile error. This is deliberate: when values cannot change unexpectedly, code is easier to reason about, especially with threads. When a value must change, say so with `mut`: `let mut count = 0;`. Reading `mut` in code tells you exactly which values move.

**Constants** (`const MAX_POINTS: u32 = 100_000;`) are always immutable, must have a type annotation, can be declared in any scope including globally, and must be set to a value computable at compile time. They are named in UPPER_SNAKE_CASE. Underscores in numbers are only for readability.

**Shadowing** declares a new variable with the same name as an old one: `let spaces = "   "; let spaces = spaces.len();`. The second `let` creates a new binding (even of a different type) and the old one is hidden. That is different from `mut`: shadowing makes a new variable each time and the result is still immutable, which is handy for transforming a value step by step (trim, then parse) without inventing names like `spaces_str` and `spaces_num`. Shadowing inside an inner block ends when the block ends.
how: `let x = 5;` immutable; `let mut x = 5;` mutable.
`const NAME: Type = value;` for compile-time constants, any scope.

idea: Rust's **scalar types** are single values: integers, floating-point numbers, booleans and characters. Integers come in signed (`i8`, `i16`, `i32`, `i64`, `i128`, `isize`) and unsigned (`u8` … `u128`, `usize`) sizes; the number is the width in bits, and `isize`/`usize` match the machine's pointer size (used for indexes and lengths). Without other information, integers default to `i32` and floats to `f64`.

Every integer type has a fixed range, so arithmetic can **overflow**: `255u8 + 1` does not fit. In debug builds Rust panics on overflow; in release builds it wraps around silently. When overflow is possible and you care, say what you want explicitly: `checked_add` returns `None` on overflow, `saturating_add` clamps to the maximum, `wrapping_add` wraps, and `overflowing_add` returns the result and a flag.

Floats (`f32`, `f64`) follow IEEE 754, with the usual surprises (`0.1 + 0.2` is not exactly `0.3`). Integer division truncates towards zero (`-7 / 2 == -3`) and `%` gives the remainder. Rust **never converts numbers implicitly**: adding an `i32` to an `f64` is a compile error, and you convert with `as` (which can truncate) or the safer `From`/`TryFrom`. A `bool` is `true` or `false`. A `char` is a single Unicode scalar value, 4 bytes, written in single quotes: `'a'`, `'é'`, `'🦀'`.
how: Integers default to `i32`, floats to `f64`; suffixes like `10u8` or `2.5f32` pick a type.

idea: **Compound types** group several values. A **tuple** holds a fixed number of values of possibly different types: `let point: (i32, f64, char) = (3, 1.5, 'x');`. Read the parts by **destructuring** (`let (x, y, z) = point;`) or by position with `.0`, `.1`, `.2`. The empty tuple `()` is called **unit**: it is the value of expressions that return nothing, such as a function with no return value. Functions often return tuples to give back several results at once.

An **array** holds a fixed number of values of the **same** type, stored next to each other: `let days = ["Mon", "Tue", "Wed"];` has type `[&str; 3]`; the length is part of the type. `[0; 5]` creates five zeros. Arrays live on the stack and are ideal when the size is known and fixed (the months of the year, a 3×3 grid). When the size changes at run time, use a `Vec` (chapter 8).

Indexing an array is **bounds-checked**: `days[10]` does not read random memory, as it might in C; it panics with a clear message. When an index may be out of range, `days.get(10)` returns an `Option` (`None` instead of a panic). Iterate with `for day in days` or `for (i, day) in days.iter().enumerate()`.

idea: Functions are declared with `fn`, take **typed parameters** and declare a return type after an arrow: `fn area(width: f64, height: f64) -> f64`. Parameter types are always required (Rust does not infer them across function boundaries), which makes every function signature a precise contract. Names use snake_case.

Rust distinguishes **statements** from **expressions**. A statement performs an action and returns nothing: `let x = 5;` is a statement. An expression evaluates to a value: `5 + 1`, a function call, a block `{ ... }`, an `if`, a `match`. The key rule: a block's value is its **last expression**, written **without a semicolon**. Adding a semicolon turns it into a statement whose value is `()`.

So a function returns the value of its final expression: `fn square(x: i32) -> i32 { x * x }`. The `return` keyword exists for leaving early (`if n < 0 { return 0; }`), but the idiomatic style ends with a bare expression. This expression-oriented design is why `let y = if x > 0 { 1 } else { -1 };` and `let total = { let a = 2; a * 3 };` work: blocks and `if` produce values.

`return value;` for early exits.

No return type means the function returns `()`.

idea: Rust's control flow is built from expressions. **`if`/`else`** takes a condition that must be a `bool` (no truthiness: `if count` is an error; write `if count != 0`). There are three loops. **`loop`** repeats forever until `break`, and `break value` makes the loop itself evaluate to that value, which is handy for retrying until something succeeds. **`while`** repeats while a condition holds. **`for`** iterates over anything iterable: arrays, ranges (`for i in 1..=10`), and later vectors, maps and iterator chains; it is the safest and most common loop, because it cannot go out of bounds. `.rev()` iterates backwards.

Nested loops can be **labelled**: `'outer: for ...` lets an inner `break 'outer;` or `continue 'outer;` jump out of or continue the outer loop directly, instead of juggling flag variables. Prefer `for` over `while` with an index counter: `while i < arr.len()` with manual indexing is slower (bounds checks on each access) and easier to get wrong.

idea: **Ownership** is how Rust manages memory without a garbage collector and without manual `free`. Three rules: every value has exactly one **owner** (a variable); there is only one owner at a time; when the owner goes out of scope, the value is **dropped** and its memory freed. The compiler checks these rules at compile time, so they cost nothing at run time.

The rules matter most for data on the **heap**. A `String` is three words on the stack (a pointer, a length and a capacity) pointing at text stored on the heap. If `let s2 = s1;` copied only those three words, both variables would point at the same heap memory and both would try to free it. Rust's answer is the **move**: after `let s2 = s1;`, `s1` is no longer valid, ownership has moved to `s2`, and using `s1` is a compile error. Nothing is copied on the heap; only the three stack words move.

When you really want two independent copies, ask for one with **`.clone()`**, which duplicates the heap data (and is visibly a potentially costly operation). Simple values that live entirely on the stack, like integers, floats, booleans, chars and tuples of them, implement the **`Copy`** trait: assignment copies them and both variables stay usable, because copying a few bytes is cheap and there is nothing to free twice.

idea: Function calls follow the same ownership rules as assignment. Passing a `String` to a function **moves** it into the parameter: the function now owns it, and when the function ends the value is dropped, so the caller can no longer use it. Passing an integer **copies** it, and the caller keeps using its own.

Return values move ownership back out. A function that creates a `String` and returns it hands ownership to the caller; a function can also take ownership, use the value and give it back. That works, but threading every value in and out of functions (`let (s, len) = calculate_length(s);`) quickly becomes clumsy.

The usual solution is **borrowing**, the next lesson: pass a reference so the function can use the value without owning it. Taking ownership is still the right choice when the function genuinely needs to keep the value (storing it in a struct, sending it to another thread) or consume it (turning it into something else). A good guideline when designing functions: borrow (`&T`) to read, borrow mutably (`&mut T`) to modify in place, take by value (`T`) only to keep or consume.

idea: A **reference** lets you use a value without owning it. `&s` creates a shared reference (a **borrow**); a function parameter `text: &String` (or better `&str`) receives it, and the caller keeps ownership: nothing is moved and nothing is dropped when the function returns. To modify a borrowed value, use a **mutable reference**, `&mut s`, which requires the variable itself to be `mut`.

The **borrowing rules**, checked at compile time, are what make Rust memory-safe and free of data races: at any moment you can have **either** any number of shared references (`&T`) **or** exactly one mutable reference (`&mut T`), never both; and references must always be **valid**, never outliving the value they point to. "Many readers or one writer" means no part of the program can change data while another part is reading it.

The rules apply to where references are actually used, not to where they are written (this is called non-lexical lifetimes): a shared reference's borrow ends after its last use, so you can create a mutable reference afterwards in the same scope. And because a reference can never outlive its value, **dangling references** are impossible: returning a reference to a local variable is a compile error.

idea: A **slice** is a reference to a contiguous part of a collection: a view, not a copy. A **string slice**, `&str`, points into some UTF-8 text: `&s[0..5]` refers to the first five bytes of `s`. It is a pointer plus a length, so creating one is free, and because it is a reference, the borrowing rules keep it valid: you cannot clear a `String` while a slice into it is still in use.

String **literals** are slices too: `"hello"` has type `&'static str`, a slice pointing into text baked into the program binary. That is why idiomatic functions take `&str` rather than `&String`: a `&str` parameter accepts literals, whole Strings (via `&s`, thanks to automatic deref coercion) and parts of Strings, while `&String` accepts only the second.

Range syntax mirrors the rest of the language: `&s[..3]`, `&s[2..]`, `&s[..]`. Slice ranges are in **bytes**, and must fall on character boundaries: slicing `"café"` at byte 4 splits the `é` (two bytes) and panics. For text, prefer methods that work in characters or words (`split_whitespace`, `chars`, `find`). Other collections have slices too: `&v[1..3]` on a `Vec<i32>` or an array is a `&[i32]`, and functions that take `&[T]` accept arrays, vectors and parts of them alike.

idea: A **struct** groups related values under one name, with a **named field** for each: `struct User { name: String, email: String, active: bool, logins: u64 }`. Create an instance by giving every field a value, in any order, and read or (if the binding is `mut`) change fields with dot notation. Mutability applies to the whole instance; Rust has no per-field `mut`.

Two shortcuts reduce repetition. **Field init shorthand**: when a variable has the same name as a field, write `User { name, email, active: true, logins: 0 }`. **Struct update syntax**: `User { email: new_email, ..other }` takes the remaining fields from another instance; note that this moves any non-Copy fields (like `String`s) out of `other`.

Two other shapes exist. **Tuple structs** have a name but unnamed fields (`struct Rgb(u8, u8, u8);`), useful to give a distinct type to a plain tuple: an `Rgb` and a `Point3(u8, u8, u8)` cannot be mixed up even though their contents match. **Unit-like structs** have no fields at all (`struct AlwaysEqual;`) and are used to implement traits on a type that holds no data. Structs usually **own** their data (`String` rather than `&str`), so an instance is valid for as long as it exists; holding references requires lifetimes (chapter 10).

Unit-like structs: `struct Marker;`.
Own the data (`String`, `Vec`) unless you need references and lifetimes.

idea: The Book's rectangle program shows why structs matter by refactoring the same calculation three times. Version one passes `width` and `height` as two loose parameters: nothing says they belong together. Version two uses a tuple `(u32, u32)`: grouped, but `dims.0` and `dims.1` hide which is which, so swapping them is an easy, silent bug. Version three defines `struct Rectangle { width: u32, height: u32 }` and passes `&Rectangle`: grouped and labelled, and the function signature now reads like the problem.

Printing a struct needs a format. `{}` uses the `Display` trait, which you write by hand when there is a sensible user-facing form. For developers, add `#[derive(Debug)]` and print with `{:?}`, or `{:#?}` for a pretty, multi-line layout.

The **`dbg!`** macro is the debugging companion: `dbg!(expression)` prints the file, line, the expression's source text and its value to standard error, then **returns** the value, so it can wrap part of a larger expression without changing the program (`let area = dbg!(width * 2) * height;`). idea: **Methods** are functions defined inside an `impl` block for a type, whose first parameter is `self`. They are called with dot syntax (`rect.area()`), and the type of `self` says what the method does with the instance: `&self` borrows it to read (most common), `&mut self` borrows it to modify, and plain `self` takes ownership, consuming the instance (useful when transforming it into something else). Rust automatically adds `&`, `&mut` or `*` at the call site to match, so you always write `rect.area()`.

Methods can take extra parameters after `self`: `rect.can_hold(&other)`. Grouping behaviour with the data in `impl` blocks also organises code: everything you can do with a `Rectangle` is in one place, and other code finds it by typing `rect.` in an editor.

Functions in an `impl` block that do **not** take `self` are **associated functions**, called with `::` on the type: `Rectangle::square(10)`. They are most often **constructors**; by convention `new` is the standard constructor, but descriptive names (`square`, `from_config`, `with_capacity`) are common and clearer. Inside an `impl`, `Self` is an alias for the type. A type can have several `impl` blocks.
how: `impl Type { fn method(&self) ... }`; call `value.method()`.
`&self` to read, `&mut self` to modify, `self` to consume.
Extra parameters follow `self`: `fn can_hold(&self, other: &Rectangle) -> bool`.
Associated functions (no `self`): `fn new(...) -> Self`, called `Type::new(...)`.
`Self` refers to the type inside its `impl`.

idea: An **enum** defines a type by listing its possible **variants**: a value is exactly one of them. `enum IpAddr { V4(u8, u8, u8, u8), V6(String) }` says an address is either a version 4 address holding four bytes or a version 6 address holding a string. Unlike enums in many languages, each Rust variant can carry **its own data**, of different shapes: none, a tuple, or named fields. That makes enums perfect for modelling "one of several kinds of thing", such as messages, commands, events or states.
Enums can have methods in `impl` blocks, just like structs, and they are usually handled with `match` (next lesson), which forces you to deal with every variant.

The most important enum in the standard library is **`Option<T>`**: `Some(value)` or `None`. Rust has **no null**: a value that might be missing has type `Option<T>`, which is a different type from `T`, so the compiler stops you from using it as if it were always present. To get at the inner value you must handle the `None` case, with `match`, `if let`, or methods like `unwrap_or`, `map` and `?`. The billion-dollar mistake of null-pointer errors becomes a compile-time check.

idea: **`match`** compares a value against a series of **patterns** and runs the code of the first arm that matches. Each arm is `pattern => expression`, and the whole `match` is an expression, so it can produce a value. Patterns can be literal values, variable names, wildcards and, most powerfully, enum variants that **bind** the data inside them: `Coin::Quarter(state) => ...` gives you the `state` stored in that variant.

Matching is **exhaustive**: the compiler checks that every possible value is covered and refuses the program otherwise. For enums like `Option` this means you cannot forget the `None` case; for integers or strings, where listing every value is impossible, finish with a **catch-all**: a variable name (`other => ...`) if you need the value, or `_` if you do not. Arms are checked in order, so put specific patterns before general ones (a catch-all first would make the rest unreachable, and the compiler warns).

Arms can have multiple patterns with `|` (`1 | 2 => ...`), ranges (`1..=9`), and **guards**: extra conditions after `if` (`Some(n) if n < 0 => ...`). An arm's expression can be a block `{ ... }` for several lines. Matching on a reference (`match &value`) binds references, leaving the value usable afterwards.

idea: Sometimes you care about just one pattern. Writing a full `match` with a `_ => ()` arm is noisy, so Rust offers **`if let`**: `if let Some(max) = config_max { println!("max is {max}"); }` runs the block only when the pattern matches, binding the value. An `else` branch handles everything else. It is the same pattern matching as `match`, minus the exhaustiveness check, a trade of thoroughness for brevity that suits "do something if present" cases.

**`let ... else`** (let-else) handles the opposite situation: you need a value to continue, and otherwise you want to leave. `let Some(user) = find_user(id) else { return Err("no such user"); };` binds `user` for the **rest of the function** (not just a block, unlike `if let`), and the `else` block must **diverge**: `return`, `break`, `continue` or panic. This keeps the "happy path" un-indented instead of nesting it inside `if let` blocks.

**`while let`** loops as long as a pattern matches, for example popping from a stack until it is empty: `while let Some(top) = stack.pop() { ... }`. Together with `match`, these four forms cover every situation: all cases (`match`), one case (`if let`), required value or leave (`let else`), and repeat while matching (`while let`).

idea: Rust code is organised in three layers. A **crate** is the smallest unit the compiler builds: either a **binary crate** (a program with a `main` function) or a **library crate** (code for other crates to use, with no `main`). Each crate has a **crate root**, the source file the compiler starts from: `src/main.rs` for the binary and `src/lib.rs` for the library. A **package** is what `cargo new` creates: a folder with a `Cargo.toml` that describes how to build one or more crates.

The rules are simple. A package can contain at most **one library** crate and any number of **binary** crates. Cargo finds them by convention, no configuration needed: `src/lib.rs` makes the library (named after the package), `src/main.rs` makes a binary with the package's name, and every file in `src/bin/` becomes an additional binary named after the file.

The common professional layout is a **library plus a thin binary**: almost all the logic lives in `src/lib.rs` (and its modules), and `src/main.rs` only parses arguments and calls the library. The library is then easy to test, reuse and document, and the binary refers to it by the package name (`use my_package::run;`) exactly as an outside crate would.

idea: **Modules** organise code inside a crate into a tree of named scopes. `mod front_of_house { ... }` declares a module; modules can nest, and the crate root is the implicit top of the tree, called `crate`. Modules group related code and, just as importantly, control **privacy**.

Everything in Rust is **private by default**: an item (function, struct, enum, module, constant) is visible only inside the module where it is defined and its children. `pub` makes an item visible to the parent module and beyond. That default lets you hide implementation details and change them freely, exposing only a small, deliberate public interface.

Privacy has two details worth remembering. For **structs**, `pub struct` makes the type public but its **fields stay private** unless each is marked `pub`; a struct with private fields can only be created through a public constructor, which is how you guarantee its fields are always valid. For **enums**, `pub enum` makes **all variants** public, because an enum with hidden variants would be unusable. Child modules can see everything in their ancestors (private items included); parents cannot see into children's private items.
how: `mod name { ... }` declares a module; nest freely.
Items are private by default; `pub` exposes them to the parent and beyond.
`pub struct` with private fields + a `pub fn new` keeps invariants.

idea: A **path** names an item in the module tree. An **absolute path** starts from the crate root with `crate::` (or from an external crate's name, like `std::`); a **relative path** starts from the current module, using `self::` (optional) or **`super::`** to go up to the parent. Choose absolute paths when code might move independently of what it uses, relative ones for tightly related modules; both are common.

Writing long paths everywhere is tiring, so **`use`** creates a shortcut in the current scope: `use std::collections::HashMap;`. The idiom is to bring **functions** in by their parent module (`use crate::util::files;` then `files::read(...)`), so a call shows where the function comes from, and to bring **structs, enums and traits** in by their full path (`use std::collections::HashMap;`). Rename on import with **`as`** when two names clash (`use std::fmt::Result as FmtResult;`). Group imports with braces and `self`: `use std::io::{self, Write};`.

**`pub use`** re-exports a name: it brings an item into scope and makes it public at the new location. Libraries use this to offer a simple, flat public API (`mylib::Config`) while keeping a deeper internal structure (`mylib::config::loader::Config`). External crates from Cargo.toml are available by name; `std` is always available.

idea: As a crate grows, modules move out of one big file into their own files. The rule is short: **`mod name;`** (with a semicolon instead of a body) tells the compiler "the contents of this module are in a file". For a module declared in the crate root, the compiler looks for **`src/name.rs`** (or the older style `src/name/mod.rs`). For a nested module `mod hosting;` declared inside `src/front_of_house.rs`, it looks in **`src/front_of_house/hosting.rs`**: the folder is named after the parent module.

Each file is declared **exactly once**, with `mod`, in its parent. `mod` is not an import: it defines where a module sits in the tree. After that, other code refers to it by path and `use`, as before. Forgetting the `mod` line is the classic mistake: the file exists, but the compiler never reads it, and `use crate::name` fails with "unresolved import".

Moving code between files never changes paths: `crate::front_of_house::hosting::add_to_waitlist` is the same whether `hosting` is inline or in a file. So you can start with everything in one file and split it later without touching any calling code. Organise modules by **feature** (orders, billing, users) rather than by kind of thing (models, utils), so a change usually touches one module.

idea: **`Vec<T>`** is a growable list of values of one type, stored next to each other on the heap. Create one with `Vec::new()` (an annotation like `Vec<i32>` is needed if nothing is pushed yet) or with the `vec![1, 2, 3]` macro. `push` adds to the end and `pop` removes from the end, returning an `Option` (`None` when empty). The vector must be `mut` to change.

Two ways to read an element: indexing `v[2]` returns the value and **panics** if the index is out of range, while `v.get(2)` returns `Option<&T>`, `None` when out of range. Use indexing when an out-of-range index is a bug, `get` when it can legitimately happen (user input).

Iterate with `for x in &v` (shared references), `for x in &mut v` (mutable references, change each element with `*x += 1`) or `for x in v` (takes ownership, consuming the vector). The borrowing rules apply to vectors as a whole: holding a reference to an element while pushing is refused, because `push` may move the whole buffer to a bigger allocation. To store different types in one vector, wrap them in an **enum** (or use trait objects, chapter 18). When a vector is dropped, all its elements are dropped too.

idea: Rust has two main string types. **`String`** is an owned, growable, heap-allocated UTF-8 buffer: you can push to it and change it. **`&str`** (a string slice) is a borrowed view into UTF-8 text owned by someone else: a `String`, or text baked into the binary for literals. Functions usually take `&str` and return `String`; `&String` converts to `&str` automatically.

Build strings with `push_str` (append a `&str`), `push` (append a `char`), `format!` (like `println!` but returning a `String`, the most readable way to combine values), or `+`, which takes ownership of its left side: `s1 + &s2` moves `s1` and reuses its buffer. `to_string()`, `String::from` and `.to_owned()` turn a `&str` into a `String`.

A Rust string is a sequence of **UTF-8 bytes**, and characters take 1 to 4 bytes each. That is why **strings cannot be indexed** with `s[0]`: a byte position does not identify a character, and returning one byte of "é" would be wrong. Instead, choose the unit you mean: `.bytes()` for raw bytes, `.chars()` for Unicode scalar values, and for user-perceived characters ("grapheme clusters", like a flag emoji or an accented letter built from two code points) the `unicode-segmentation` crate. `len()` returns the number of **bytes**.

idea: **`HashMap<K, V>`** stores values by key, with fast lookup, insertion and removal (average constant time). idea: Rust divides errors into two kinds. **Recoverable** errors, like a missing file or bad input, are expected possibilities and are returned as values with `Result` (next lesson). **Unrecoverable** errors are bugs: a condition that should be impossible, such as an index past the end or a broken invariant. For those, the program **panics**.

A panic happens when you call `panic!("message")` or when code you call panics: indexing out of bounds, `unwrap()` on `None` or `Err`, integer overflow in debug builds, division by zero. By default the panicking thread **unwinds**: it walks back up the stack, running destructors (`Drop`) so resources are released, prints the message with the file and line, and ends. A panic in `main`'s thread ends the program with a non-zero exit code.

To see how the program got there, run with **`RUST_BACKTRACE=1`**: the backtrace lists the chain of function calls, most recent first; look for the first lines that are in your own code. For smaller binaries, a release profile can switch to `panic = "abort"` in `Cargo.toml`, which ends the process immediately without unwinding. Panics are not exceptions to be caught for control flow; they signal bugs to fix.

idea: **`Result<T, E>`** is the enum for operations that can fail: `Ok(value)` on success, `Err(error)` on failure. Functions like `File::open` and `str::parse` return it, and because it is a type, the compiler makes sure callers deal with it; you cannot accidentally use a `Result` as if it were the value inside.

Handle it with `match`, matching `Ok` and `Err`, and even different **kinds** of error (`ErrorKind::NotFound` versus permission problems). Shortcuts: `unwrap()` returns the value or panics; `expect("message")` does the same with your message (prefer it); `unwrap_or(default)` and `unwrap_or_else(|e| ...)` substitute a value; `map` and `map_err` transform the success or error value.

The **`?` operator** is the workhorse for **propagating** errors. Placed after an expression returning `Result`, it gives the `Ok` value, or immediately returns the `Err` from the current function. That function must itself return a `Result` (or `Option`, for `?` on Options) with a compatible error type: `?` converts the error with `From` if needed. A chain of fallible steps then reads as a straight line: `let text = fs::read_to_string(path)?; let n: u32 = text.trim().parse()?;`. `main` can return `Result<(), Box<dyn Error>>` so `?` works there too.

idea: When should code panic and when should it return a `Result`? The default for a function that can fail is **`Result`**: it lets the caller decide, and callers know their situation better than you do. Panicking is appropriate when continuing would be wrong or dangerous: a **bug** in the program (a broken invariant, an impossible state), a violated **contract** that the caller was told about (like indexing past the end), or bad state that code cannot recover from.

`unwrap` and `expect` are acceptable in a few places: examples and prototypes, tests (a panic is a test failure), and when you have information the compiler lacks, such as parsing a hard-coded valid IP address. In that last case, `expect` should explain why it cannot fail: `"127.0.0.1".parse::<IpAddr>().expect("hard-coded address is valid")`.

The best tool is often to **encode rules in types**. Instead of checking "is this a number from 1 to 100?" in every function, create a `Guess` type whose constructor validates once (returning a `Result`, or panicking if out-of-range values are a programming error), with a private field so no other code can create an invalid one. Every function that takes a `Guess` then knows the value is valid, and the check is never forgotten or duplicated. This "parse, don't validate" approach is one of the most powerful habits in Rust.

idea: **Generics** let one piece of code work with many types. Instead of writing `largest_i32`, `largest_f64` and `largest_char`, write `fn largest<T: PartialOrd>(list: &[T]) -> &T` once. `<T>` declares a **type parameter**, and the **bound** `T: PartialOrd` says what the code needs from it: here, the ability to compare with `>`. Without the bound, the compiler refuses, because it cannot assume an arbitrary `T` supports comparison.

Structs, enums and methods can be generic too: `struct Point<T> { x: T, y: T }` holds two values of the same type, and `Point<T, U>` allows different ones. `Option<T>` and `Result<T, E>` are generic enums you already use. In an `impl<T> Point<T>` block, methods work for every `T`; an `impl Point<f64>` block adds methods only for one concrete type (`distance_from_origin` makes sense for floats, not for strings).

Generics cost **nothing at run time**. The compiler performs **monomorphisation**: for each concrete type you actually use, it generates a specialised copy of the code, as if you had written `largest_i32` and `largest_char` by hand. You get the convenience of writing code once with the speed of hand-written specialised code; the price is slightly longer compile times and larger binaries.

idea: A **trait** defines behaviour that types can share: a set of method signatures, like an interface. `trait Summary { fn summarize(&self) -> String; }` says "anything that implements Summary can produce a summary". Each type provides its own implementation in an `impl Summary for Article` block. Traits can also provide **default methods** with a body, which implementors get for free and may override; a default method can call other methods of the trait, so implementing one small required method can unlock several.

Traits become powerful as **bounds**. A function parameter `item: &impl Summary` accepts any type that implements the trait; the longer form `fn notify<T: Summary>(item: &T)` means the same and is needed when two parameters must be the same type. Combine traits with `+` (`T: Summary + Display`), and move long bounds into a **`where` clause** for readability. Returning `impl Trait` hides the concrete type behind the trait, which is essential for closures and iterators.

One rule keeps the ecosystem coherent, the **orphan rule**: you can implement a trait for a type only if the trait or the type is defined in your crate. You can implement `Display` for your `Article`, or your `Summary` for `Vec<T>`, but not the standard `Display` for the standard `Vec`. Many useful traits can be **derived** automatically: `#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq, Hash, Default)]`.

idea: Every reference has a **lifetime**: the part of the program during which it is valid. Usually the compiler infers lifetimes and you never see them. The **borrow checker** compares lifetimes to guarantee that no reference outlives the data it points to, which is how Rust rules out dangling references entirely.

Sometimes the compiler needs help. In `fn longest(x: &str, y: &str) -> &str`, the returned reference comes from either `x` or `y`, and the compiler cannot know which, so it cannot check callers. **Lifetime annotations** describe the relationship: `fn longest<'a>(x: &'a str, y: &'a str) -> &'a str` says "the result lives at least as long as the shorter of the two inputs". Annotations do not change how long anything lives; they **describe** constraints so the compiler can check them at every call site. A caller that uses the result after one of the inputs has been dropped is rejected.

Structs that **hold references** need annotations too: `struct Excerpt<'a> { part: &'a str }` means an Excerpt cannot outlive the text it borrows from. Three **elision rules** let you omit annotations in the common cases (one input reference, or a method with `&self`), which is why most functions never show them. idea: Real signatures often combine all three tools: type parameters, trait bounds and lifetimes. Reading them is a skill: take each part in turn. In `fn longest_with_note<'a, T>(x: &'a str, y: &'a str, note: T) -> &'a str where T: Display`, the angle brackets declare a lifetime `'a` and a type `T`; the parameters say `x` and `y` are borrowed for `'a` and `note` is any displayable value; the return borrows for `'a`; the `where` clause states the bound. Lifetimes come first in the list, by convention.

The combination shines in data structures that **borrow** and work with **any type**. A `struct Labelled<'a, T> { label: &'a str, value: T }` can wrap anything while borrowing its label; an `impl<'a, T: Display> Labelled<'a, T>` gives it methods for displayable values. Generic functions over slices of references, such as "find the longest item that matches a predicate", naturally carry all three.

The compiler checks each part independently: bounds say what operations `T` supports, lifetimes say how long references remain valid, and the types make sure everything fits. When a signature gets hard to read, a `where` clause, descriptive type parameter names (`Item` instead of `T`) and a short doc comment help more than clever tricks.

idea: A **test** in Rust is a function annotated with `#[test]`. `cargo test` compiles your code in test mode, runs every test function (in parallel by default), and reports which passed and failed. A test fails when it panics, so checks are macros that panic on failure: `assert!(condition)`, `assert_eq!(left, right)` and `assert_ne!(left, right)`. The `_eq` forms print both values when they differ, which makes failures easy to diagnose; add a custom message after the values: `assert_eq!(total, 30, "total for {items:?}")`.

Tests usually live in a module annotated `#[cfg(test)]` at the bottom of the file, with `use super::*;` to see the code under test. The `cfg(test)` attribute means the module is only compiled for `cargo test`, so tests add nothing to the release binary.

To check that code panics when it should, add `#[should_panic]`, ideally with `expected = "part of the message"` so the test fails if it panics for the wrong reason. Tests can also return `Result<(), E>`: returning `Err` fails the test, and the `?` operator works inside, which is convenient for tests that call fallible functions.

idea: `cargo test` accepts options for itself and, after `--`, for the **test binary**. The most useful ones change what runs and what you see. idea: Rust projects use two kinds of tests. **Unit tests** sit next to the code they test, inside a `#[cfg(test)] mod tests` in the same file. Because a child module can see its parent's private items, unit tests can test **private functions** too, which is handy for tricky internal helpers.

**Integration tests** live in the `tests/` folder at the top of the package, one crate per file. They use your library exactly as an outside user would: only its **public API**, imported by the package name (`use mylib::parse;`). No `#[cfg(test)]` is needed; Cargo compiles them only for `cargo test`. They catch problems unit tests miss: a function you forgot to make public, or modules that work alone but not together.

Shared setup code for integration tests goes in **`tests/common/mod.rs`** (not `tests/common.rs`, which Cargo would treat as a test file of its own) and is pulled in with `mod common;`. Binary crates cannot be tested this way, because a binary exposes no API, which is another reason to keep logic in `src/lib.rs` with a thin `src/main.rs`. `cargo test --test name` runs one integration test file.

idea: The chapter's project is **minigrep**, a small version of the classic `grep` tool: `minigrep QUERY FILE` prints every line of the file that contains the query. It brings together much of the first half of the book: command-line arguments, files, strings, error handling, modules and tests.

idea: The refactoring separates **concerns**. Argument parsing moves into a `Config` struct with a `build` function: `Config::build(&args) -> Result<Config, &'static str>`. It checks there are enough arguments and returns `Err("not enough arguments")` instead of panicking. Grouping `query` and `file_path` in a struct also documents that they belong together.

The program logic moves into **`run(config) -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>>`**: read the file with `?`, search, print. `Box<dyn Error>` means "any kind of error", so `run` can propagate I/O errors (and later others) with `?` without defining an error type yet.

`main` becomes a thin shell: build the config, call `run`, and turn any error into a message on standard error and a non-zero exit code with **`process::exit(1)`**. `unwrap_or_else(|err| { ...; process::exit(1) })` handles the config error in one expression, and `if let Err(e) = run(config)` handles the run error. Finally, `Config` and `run` move into **`src/lib.rs`**, so they can be tested, while `src/main.rs` keeps only the wiring. This structure (parse, run, report) suits almost every command-line program.

idea: The search logic is developed **test first**. Write a test describing the behaviour (given this query and these contents, the result is exactly these lines), watch it fail, then write just enough code to make it pass. The test pins down details before you write them: does "duct" match "productive"? (Yes: it is a substring search.)

The function signature needs an explicit **lifetime**: `pub fn search<'a>(query: &str, contents: &'a str) -> Vec<&'a str>`. The returned lines are slices of `contents`, not of `query`, and the annotation tells the compiler exactly that: the results live as long as `contents`. Without it, the compiler cannot tell which input the returned references borrow from and asks for the annotation. Returning slices instead of new Strings avoids copying every matching line.

The implementation is a loop: for each line in `contents.lines()`, if `line.contains(query)`, push it onto a result vector. Once the test passes, `run` calls `search` and prints each result. Because `search` takes text, not a file name, it is easy to test with string literals, a design that falls out naturally when tests come first.

idea: A **closure** is an anonymous function you can store in a variable or pass to another function, and unlike a regular `fn`, it can **capture** values from the scope where it is defined: `let limit = 10; let small = |n: i32| n < limit;`. Closures are written with pipes around the parameters, and types are usually **inferred**, though you can annotate them. Once inferred for a closure, the types are fixed: calling it first with an `i32` and then with a `String` is an error.

A closure captures each variable in the least demanding way its body allows: by **shared reference** if it only reads, by **mutable reference** if it changes the variable, and by **value** (moving it in) if it consumes it. The `move` keyword forces capture by value, which is required when the closure must outlive the current scope, such as a closure passed to a new thread.

How a closure captures determines which **`Fn` traits** it implements, and functions that take closures state which they need. **`FnOnce`**: can be called at least once (every closure; one that moves a captured value out can only be called once). **`FnMut`**: can be called repeatedly and may mutate captured state. **`Fn`**: can be called repeatedly without mutating anything. `unwrap_or_else` takes an `FnOnce`, `sort_by_key` an `FnMut`, and a function you call from several threads would need `Fn`.

idea: An **iterator** produces a sequence of values one at a time. The `Iterator` trait requires one method, `next(&mut self) -> Option<Self::Item>`, returning `Some(item)` until the sequence is exhausted and then `None`. `for` loops call `next` for you. Collections offer three ways to iterate: `iter()` yields shared references, `iter_mut()` mutable references, and `into_iter()` owned values, consuming the collection.

Iterator methods come in two kinds. **Iterator adaptors** (`map`, `filter`, `enumerate`, `zip`, `skip`, `take`, `rev`, `chain`, `flat_map`...) wrap an iterator in a new one and are **lazy**: nothing happens until something consumes them, and the compiler warns about an unused adaptor chain. **Consuming adaptors** (`sum`, `count`, `collect`, `max`, `min_by_key`, `fold`, `any`, `all`, `find`, `position`...) call `next` until done and produce a result. `collect` can build a `Vec`, `String`, `HashMap` and more; tell it which with a type annotation or the turbofish (`collect::<Vec<_>>()`).

Chains of adaptors read like a description of the computation (`filter` the valid ones, `map` to prices, `sum`), and because of laziness and inlining they compile to code as fast as a hand-written loop. Your own types become iterators by implementing `next`, and then get every adaptor for free.
how: `iter()` → `&T`, `iter_mut()` → `&mut T`, `into_iter()` → `T`.
Adaptors are lazy: `map`, `filter`, `enumerate`, `zip`, `take`, `skip`, `rev`, `chain`, `flat_map`.
Consumers: `sum`, `count`, `collect`, `fold`, `any`, `all`, `find`, `max_by_key`, `position`.
`collect::<Vec<_>>()` or annotate the target type.

idea: With closures and iterators, minigrep gets cleaner. `Config::build` used to take `&[String]` and **clone** the query and file path, because it could not take ownership of strings inside a borrowed slice. Instead, it can take the **argument iterator itself**: `fn build(mut args: impl Iterator<Item = String>) -> Result<Config, &'static str>`. Calling `args.next()` hands over owned Strings directly, skipping the program name and returning a clear error when an argument is missing (`match args.next() { Some(arg) => arg, None => return Err(...) }`). No clones, and `main` passes `env::args()` straight in.

`search` becomes a single expression: `contents.lines().filter(|line| line.contains(query)).collect()`. It says what it does, has no mutable state, and is easier to change (adding `.map(str::trim)` or making it lazy is one step).

Is the iterator version slower? The Book benchmarks it, and the answer is no: iterators are a **zero-cost abstraction**. The compiler inlines the closures and adaptors and often produces exactly the machine code of the hand-written loop, sometimes better, because it can drop bounds checks and unroll loops. Write the clear version, and measure if performance matters.

idea: Cargo builds with **profiles**: predefined sets of compiler settings. `dev` (used by `cargo build` and `cargo run`) compiles fast with no optimisation (`opt-level = 0`) and full debug info, ideal while writing code. `release` (`cargo build --release`) optimises heavily (`opt-level = 3`), takes longer to compile and produces much faster programs, so it is what you ship and benchmark. Override settings in `Cargo.toml` under `[profile.dev]` or `[profile.release]`: for example `opt-level = 1` in dev for faster tests, or `lto = true` and `codegen-units = 1` in release for a little more speed.

Rust has special comments for **documentation**. `///` documents the item that follows (function, struct, method) using **Markdown**, and `//!` documents the enclosing item, usually the crate or module at the top of `lib.rs`. `cargo doc --open` turns them into an HTML site like the standard library's, including your dependencies' docs.

By convention, doc comments use **sections**: `# Examples` (the most important), `# Panics` (when the function panics), `# Errors` (what errors a `Result` can contain and why), and `# Safety` (for `unsafe` functions). Code blocks inside doc comments are **doc tests**: `cargo test` compiles and runs them, so examples in documentation are guaranteed to stay correct.
how: Profiles: `dev` (fast compile) and `release` (fast program); customise in `[profile.*]`.
`///` for the next item, `//!` for the enclosing crate or module; Markdown inside.
Sections: `# Examples`, `# Panics`, `# Errors`, `# Safety`.

[profile.release]

idea: Publishing a library to **crates.io** shares it with every Rust user through `cargo add`. Before publishing, shape the **public API**. Your internal module structure may be deep (`art::kinds::PrimaryColor`, `art::utils::mix`), which is awkward for users. **`pub use`** re-exports the important items at the crate root, so users write `use art::{PrimaryColor, mix};`, and the docs list them on the front page, while you keep organising internals however you like.

crates.io requires **metadata** in `Cargo.toml`: a unique `name`, a `version`, a `description`, a `license` (an SPDX identifier such as `"MIT OR Apache-2.0"`, the Rust ecosystem's common dual licence), and usually `repository`, `readme`, `keywords` and `categories`. `cargo publish --dry-run` checks everything without uploading, and `cargo package --list` shows exactly which files will be included.

Publishing is **permanent**: a version can never be overwritten or deleted, so that crates depending on it never break. Publish fixes as a new version, following semantic versioning (a breaking change in a 1.x crate means 2.0.0). If a release is broken, **`cargo yank --vers 1.0.1`** stops new projects from selecting it, while existing projects with that version in their `Cargo.lock` keep working. Log in once with an API token from crates.io (`cargo login`).
how: Re-export with `pub use` at the crate root for a flat, convenient API.
Required metadata: `description`, `license` (SPDX), plus `repository`, `readme`, `keywords`, `categories`.

idea: As a project grows into several related crates (a library, a command-line tool, a web server sharing the same core), a **workspace** keeps them together. A workspace is a folder with a top-level `Cargo.toml` containing a `[workspace]` section listing its **members**; each member is an ordinary package in its own folder. All members share **one `Cargo.lock`** (so they agree on dependency versions) and **one `target/` directory** (so shared dependencies are compiled once).

Members depend on each other **by path**: `adder` depends on `add_one = { path = "../add_one" }`. Commands run from the workspace root apply to everything (`cargo build`, `cargo test`), and `-p name` targets one member (`cargo run -p adder`, `cargo test -p add_one`). Common settings can be inherited: `[workspace.package]` for version and edition, `[workspace.dependencies]` for shared dependency versions that members reference with `serde.workspace = true`.

Two more Cargo features round out the picture. **`cargo install`** builds a binary crate from crates.io (or a path or git repository) and puts it in `~/.cargo/bin`, the standard way to install Rust tools like `ripgrep` or `cargo-watch`. And Cargo is **extensible**: any program named `cargo-something` on your PATH can be run as `cargo something`, which is how `cargo watch`, `cargo audit` and `cargo nextest` work.
how: Root `Cargo.toml`: `[workspace] members = ["adder", "add_one"]`, `resolver = "3"`.
Path dependencies between members: `add_one = { path = "../add_one" }`.
One `Cargo.lock` and `target/` for all members.
`cargo build`, `cargo test` at the root; `-p name` for one member.

idea: A **smart pointer** is a struct that acts like a pointer but carries extra capabilities and ownership rules. `String` and `Vec` are smart pointers; the chapter adds the general-purpose ones. The simplest is **`Box<T>`**: it stores a value on the **heap** and keeps only a pointer on the stack. `let b = Box::new(5);` works like any value: it is dropped (stack pointer and heap data) when it goes out of scope, and you use it like the value inside thanks to dereferencing.

Box has three main uses. First, **recursive types**: a type that contains itself, like a cons list (`List::Cons(1, rest)`) or a tree node with children. Rust must know every type's size at compile time, and a type that contains itself directly would be infinitely large; a `Box<List>` field is just a pointer of known size, which breaks the recursion. Second, **large values** you want to move without copying many bytes: moving a Box moves only the pointer. Third, **trait objects**, `Box<dyn Trait>`, holding values of different types behind one interface (chapter 18).
Box has no run-time overhead beyond the heap allocation itself, and none of the extra features of `Rc` or `RefCell`. Reach for it when you need indirection or heap allocation with a single owner.
how: `Box::new(value)` puts the value on the heap; `*b` dereferences.
Recursive types: `enum List { Cons(i32, Box<List>), Nil }`.

Moving a Box moves only the pointer.

idea: Two traits make smart pointers feel like the values they hold. **`Deref`** lets a type behave like a reference: implementing `fn deref(&self) -> &Self::Target` makes `*my_box` work, and Rust inserts that call for you. More importantly, it enables **deref coercion**: when a function expects `&str` and you pass `&String` (or `&Box<String>`), Rust applies `deref` as many times as needed to make the types match. That is why `&String` works wherever `&str` is expected, and why you rarely write `&*` by hand. `DerefMut` does the same for mutable references.

**`Drop`** customises what happens when a value goes out of scope: implement `fn drop(&mut self)` and Rust calls it automatically, which is how Box frees its heap memory, files close themselves and locks release. Values are dropped in **reverse order** of declaration, so things created later, which may depend on earlier ones, are cleaned up first.

You cannot call `drop` as a method yourself (that would risk a double free when Rust calls it again at the end of scope). To clean up early, call the function **`std::mem::drop(value)`** (in the prelude as `drop`), which takes ownership and lets the value go out of scope immediately: useful for releasing a lock or closing a file before the end of a function.
how: `impl Deref for T { type Target = U; fn deref(&self) -> &U { ... } }`.
Deref coercion: `&String` → `&str`, `&Box<T>` → `&T`, automatically.
`impl Drop for T { fn drop(&mut self) { ... } }` for cleanup.

`drop(value)` releases early; `value.drop()` is not allowed.

idea: Sometimes one value genuinely has **several owners**: a node in a graph pointed to by many edges, or a shared configuration used by many parts of a program, where nobody can say which part will finish last. **`Rc<T>`** (reference counted) enables this for single-threaded code. `Rc::new(value)` puts the value on the heap with a counter; **`Rc::clone(&rc)`** creates another owner by incrementing the counter, without copying the data. When an owner is dropped the count goes down, and when it reaches zero the value itself is dropped.

`Rc::strong_count(&rc)` shows how many owners exist, which is handy for learning and debugging. The convention is to write `Rc::clone(&a)` rather than `a.clone()`, to make it obvious at a glance that this is a cheap pointer copy, not a deep clone.

Rc gives **shared, read-only** access: you cannot get a `&mut T` from an `Rc<T>`, because several owners modifying the same data would break the borrowing rules. Combine it with `RefCell` (next lesson) when shared data must change. Rc is **not thread-safe** (its counter is not atomic), and the compiler stops you from sending it to another thread; the thread-safe equivalent is `Arc` (chapter 16).

`Rc::strong_count(&a)` shows the number of owners.
The value is dropped when the last Rc is dropped.

idea: The borrowing rules are normally checked at compile time. **`RefCell<T>`** moves the check to **run time**: it allows **interior mutability**, changing data through a shared reference, while still enforcing "many readers or one writer". `cell.borrow()` returns a `Ref<T>` (a shared borrow) and `cell.borrow_mut()` a `RefMut<T>` (a mutable borrow); RefCell counts the active borrows, and if you break the rules, for example by calling `borrow_mut` while another borrow is alive, the program **panics** instead of refusing to compile.

Why give up compile-time checking? Some correct designs are impossible to express statically. A classic case is a **mock object** in tests: a trait method takes `&self`, but the mock needs to record each call, which means mutating itself. With a `RefCell<Vec<String>>` field, the mock can push messages through `&self`. For simple Copy values, `Cell<T>` offers `get`/`set` with no borrowing at all.

Combining **`Rc<RefCell<T>>`** gives **shared, mutable** data with several owners: each owner can borrow mutably when needed, one at a time. It is powerful but moves errors to run time, so keep borrows short (borrow, use, drop in one expression), and prefer plain ownership when it works. Like Rc, RefCell is single-threaded; the thread-safe counterparts are `Mutex` and `RwLock`.
how: `RefCell::new(v)`; `.borrow()` → `Ref<T>`, `.borrow_mut()` → `RefMut<T>`.
Breaking the rules panics at run time ("already borrowed").
`try_borrow_mut()` returns a Result instead of panicking.

idea: Rust's guarantees prevent memory errors, but not **memory leaks**. With `Rc` and `RefCell`, two values can point at each other: A holds an Rc to B and B holds an Rc to A. Each keeps the other's strong count above zero, so when the program drops its own references, neither count reaches zero and neither value is ever freed: a **reference cycle**.

The fix is **`Weak<T>`**, a non-owning reference. `Rc::downgrade(&rc)` creates a Weak pointer, which increments a separate `weak_count` but not the strong count, so it does not keep the value alive. To use it, call **`upgrade()`**, which returns `Option<Rc<T>>`: `Some` if the value still exists, `None` if it has been dropped. Code must handle that possibility, which is exactly right for a reference that does not own its target.

The rule of thumb for trees and graphs: **owning** relationships use `Rc` (a parent owns its children), and **back-references** use `Weak` (a child refers to its parent without owning it). Dropping the parent then frees it, and its children's `Weak` parent links simply return `None` from `upgrade`.

`weak.upgrade()` → `Option<Rc<T>>`; `None` once the value is gone.
Parents own children with `Rc`; children point to parents with `Weak`.

idea: A **thread** runs code concurrently with the rest of the program. `thread::spawn(|| { ... })` starts one with a closure and returns a **`JoinHandle`**; calling **`handle.join()`** waits for the thread to finish and returns its result (or an error if it panicked). When `main` returns, the process ends and any threads still running are stopped, so join the threads whose work you need. The order in which threads run is up to the operating system and differs between runs.

A spawned thread may outlive the function that created it, so its closure cannot borrow local variables. Rust requires a **`move` closure** that takes ownership of what it uses: `thread::spawn(move || { println!("{v:?}"); })`. The compiler explains this if you forget, because a borrow could otherwise dangle.

When threads only need to borrow data for a bounded time, **`thread::scope`** is simpler: threads spawned inside a scope are guaranteed to finish before the scope ends, so they **can** borrow local variables, even mutably for distinct parts. Rust's ownership and borrowing rules apply across threads, which is why the compiler catches data races before the program runs: the "fearless concurrency" of the chapter's title.

idea: One way for threads to cooperate is to **send messages** instead of sharing memory. A **channel** has a transmitter and a receiver: `let (tx, rx) = mpsc::channel();`. Any thread holding `tx` can `send(value)`, and the thread holding `rx` receives values in the order they were sent. `mpsc` means multiple producer, single consumer: **clone the transmitter** (`tx.clone()`) to give one to each producer thread.

Sending **moves** the value into the channel: after `tx.send(report)`, the sending thread can no longer use `report`. That is ownership doing its job: two threads can never both access the same value, so no lock is needed.

On the receiving side, **`recv()`** blocks until a value arrives, returning `Ok(value)`, or `Err` once every transmitter has been dropped and the channel is empty; `try_recv()` returns immediately; and the receiver can be used as an **iterator** (`for msg in rx`), which ends automatically when all senders are gone. That makes dropping the senders the natural "no more work" signal; forgetting to drop the original `tx` in the main thread is a classic reason for a program that hangs forever. `mpsc::sync_channel(n)` creates a bounded channel whose `send` blocks when it is full.

`tx.send(v)` moves `v` into the channel; returns Err if the receiver is gone.

idea: The other way to cooperate is **shared state** protected by a lock. A **`Mutex<T>`** (mutual exclusion) wraps data so that only one thread at a time can access it. `mutex.lock()` waits until the lock is free and returns a **`MutexGuard`**, a smart pointer to the data; when the guard is dropped (at the end of its scope), the lock is released automatically. You cannot forget to unlock, and you cannot reach the data without locking, because the data is inside the Mutex.

To share one Mutex between threads, it needs several owners. `Rc` is not thread-safe, so Rust provides **`Arc<T>`** (atomically reference counted): the same idea with an atomic counter, safe to clone across threads. `Arc<Mutex<T>>` is the standard pattern for shared mutable state.

`lock()` returns a `Result`: if a thread panicked while holding the lock, the Mutex is **poisoned**, and other threads get an error, since the data may be half-updated; most code calls `.unwrap()` or `.expect()`. Keep critical sections **short** (lock, update, release) to avoid slowing other threads, and beware **deadlocks**: two threads each holding one lock and waiting for the other's. Always taking locks in the same order prevents them. For simple counters, atomic types (`AtomicUsize`) avoid locks entirely.
how: `let m = Arc::new(Mutex::new(value));` clone the Arc for each thread.
`let mut guard = m.lock().unwrap(); *guard += 1;` unlocks when the guard drops.
Arc is the thread-safe Rc; Rc cannot cross threads.

idea: How does the compiler know that `Arc` is safe to share between threads but `Rc` is not? Two **marker traits** with no methods carry that information. A type is **`Send`** if ownership of a value can be **transferred** to another thread. A type is **`Sync`** if it can be **referenced** from several threads at once; precisely, `T` is Sync when `&T` is Send.

Almost every type is both, and the compiler implements them **automatically**: a struct made only of Send fields is Send, and likewise for Sync. The exceptions are deliberate. **`Rc<T>`** is neither, because two threads cloning it at the same moment could corrupt its non-atomic counter. **`RefCell<T>`** is Send but not Sync, because its borrow tracking is not thread-safe. Raw pointers are neither. Their thread-safe counterparts, `Arc`, `Mutex`, `RwLock` and the atomics, are Send and Sync.

`thread::spawn` requires its closure, and everything the closure captures, to be **Send**. So trying to move an Rc into a thread is not a run-time bug waiting to happen; it is a compile error that names the problem. You rarely implement these traits yourself: doing so requires `unsafe`, and it is only needed when building new concurrency primitives.

idea: **Async** programming lets one thread make progress on many tasks that spend most of their time **waiting**: for the network, a timer, a database. Instead of blocking a thread per task, an async function **pauses** at each wait and lets other work run, resuming when its data is ready.

The building block is a **future**: a value representing a computation that will finish later. An **`async fn`** (or an `async { ... }` block) returns a future instead of running immediately. Futures are **lazy**: nothing happens until the future is **awaited** with `.await`, which runs it until it completes, pausing the current async function at that point if it has to wait. Calling an async function without `.await` does nothing at all, and the compiler warns that the future is unused.

Futures need a **runtime** to drive them: an executor that polls futures, plus the I/O and timer machinery that wakes them up. Rust's standard library defines the `Future` trait but ships no runtime; **Tokio** is the most widely used one. `#[tokio::main]` turns `async fn main` into a normal `main` that starts the runtime and runs it. Awaiting two futures one after the other runs them **sequentially**: the second starts only after the first finishes. Running them at the same time is the next lesson.

idea: Concurrency comes from running several futures **at the same time**. **`tokio::join!(a, b, c)`** awaits several futures concurrently within the current task and returns all their results as a tuple once every one has finished; total time is about the longest, not the sum. `tokio::try_join!` does the same for futures returning `Result` and stops at the first error.

**`tokio::spawn(future)`** creates an independent **task**, scheduled by the runtime, possibly on another thread in the multi-threaded runtime. It returns a **`JoinHandle`**; awaiting it gives the task's result (wrapped in a Result that reports panics). Spawned tasks must own their data (`async move`) and be `Send + 'static`, like threads, because they may outlive the caller and move between threads. Tasks are very cheap (bytes, not megabytes like threads), so spawning thousands is normal.

Tasks communicate with **async channels**: `tokio::sync::mpsc::channel(capacity)` gives a sender and receiver whose `send(...).await` waits if the channel is full (back-pressure) and whose `recv().await` waits for a message, returning `None` once all senders are dropped. Sometimes you want the **first** result instead of all of them. **`tokio::select!`** waits on several futures and runs the branch of whichever completes first, **cancelling** (dropping) the others. Cancellation in Rust is simply dropping the future, so code after an `.await` point may never run; keep that in mind when a select branch loses.

idea: A **stream** is the asynchronous version of an iterator: it produces a sequence of values over time, each possibly after a wait. Ticks from a timer, messages from a channel, lines from a socket and rows from a database query are all streams. The `Stream` trait lives in the `futures` crate (and Tokio's `tokio-stream`), with extension traits (`StreamExt`) providing iterator-like adaptors: `next().await`, `map`, `filter`, `take`, `then` (an async map), and `collect`. Process a stream with `while let Some(item) = stream.next().await`.

Under the hood, the **`Future` trait** has one method, `poll`, which the runtime calls; it returns `Poll::Ready(value)` or `Poll::Pending` (plus a promise to wake the task later). `async fn` writes these state machines for you. Some futures must not move in memory once polled, because they hold references into themselves; **`Pin`** expresses that guarantee. You will meet `Pin` mostly in error messages and signatures (`Pin<Box<dyn Future>>`); `Box::pin(fut)` or the `pin!` macro usually solves them.

Async and threads complement each other. Async excels at many concurrent I/O waits; threads (or `spawn_blocking`, which runs work on a dedicated thread pool) suit CPU-heavy work and blocking libraries. Since Rust 1.75, traits can have `async fn` methods directly.

idea: Is Rust object-oriented? It depends on the definition. **Objects** that bundle data with behaviour: yes, structs and enums with `impl` blocks. **Encapsulation**, hiding implementation details behind a public interface: yes, with `pub` and private fields. **Inheritance**, a type reusing another type's implementation and being usable wherever its parent is: no, Rust has none.

Encapsulation is the important part, and Rust supports it fully. A struct with private fields and public methods can maintain **invariants**: an `AveragedCollection` that keeps a list and its cached average must update the average whenever the list changes, so the list is private and only `add` and `remove` methods change it. Users cannot put the struct into an inconsistent state, and the implementation can change (say, from a `Vec` to a running sum) without breaking them.

Inheritance is usually wanted for two reasons, and Rust covers both differently. **Code reuse**: trait default methods share implementations across types. **Polymorphism**, treating different types through one interface: generics with trait bounds (resolved at compile time) and **trait objects** (resolved at run time, next lesson). Many modern designs prefer composition and traits over inheritance anyway, because inheritance tends to share more code than intended.
how: Objects: structs/enums with methods in `impl` blocks.
Encapsulation: private fields, public methods that preserve invariants.
No inheritance; reuse code with trait default methods.
Polymorphism with generics (`impl Trait`) or trait objects (`dyn Trait`).
Prefer composition: structs containing other structs.

idea: A `Vec<T>` holds one type. What about a GUI screen holding buttons, text boxes and images, all of which can be drawn? **Trait objects** solve this: `Box<dyn Draw>` is a pointer to *some* value implementing `Draw`, with its concrete type erased. A `Vec<Box<dyn Draw>>` can hold a Button and a TextField side by side, and calling `component.draw()` runs the right implementation for each.

That call uses **dynamic dispatch**: a trait object is a "fat pointer" made of a pointer to the data and a pointer to a **vtable**, a table of function pointers for that type's implementation of the trait. At run time, the call looks up the method in the vtable. Generics, by contrast, use **static dispatch**: the compiler generates a specialised copy per type (monomorphisation) and calls the method directly, which allows inlining. Static dispatch is a little faster; trait objects allow **heterogeneous collections** and types chosen at run time, such as plug-ins, and keep binaries smaller.

Not every trait can become a trait object: it must be **dyn compatible** (formerly "object safe"). Roughly, its methods cannot be generic and cannot return `Self`, because the vtable needs a fixed set of concrete functions. `Clone` is the classic example of a trait that cannot be used as `dyn Clone`.
how: `Box<dyn Trait>`, `&dyn Trait` or `Rc<dyn Trait>` for a value of any implementing type.
`Vec<Box<dyn Trait>>` for heterogeneous collections.
Dynamic dispatch through a vtable; generics use static dispatch.
Choose generics for one type per use and speed; trait objects for mixed types at run time.
Dyn-compatible traits: no generic methods, no `Self` return values (or mark them `where Self: Sized`).

idea: The **state pattern** models something that moves through states, with behaviour depending on the current state. The Book's example is a blog post: a draft, then pending review, then published; only a published post shows its content. The object-oriented version stores the state as a trait object, `state: Option<Box<dyn State>>`, and each state struct implements methods like `request_review(self: Box<Self>) -> Box<dyn State>` that return the next state. The `Post` delegates to its state. Adding a state means adding a struct, and states encapsulate their own rules.

The Rust-flavoured alternative **encodes states as types**: `DraftPost`, `PendingReviewPost` and `Post` are separate structs, and transitions are methods that **consume** one and return another: `draft.request_review()` returns a `PendingReviewPost`, whose `approve()` returns a `Post`. Only `Post` has a `content()` method, so calling it on a draft is not a run-time "empty string" but a **compile error**. This "typestate" approach moves rule violations from run time to compile time.

Both are valid. Trait objects suit states chosen at run time (loaded from a database, many states, frequent additions); typestates suit workflows whose order is fixed and where mistakes should be impossible to compile.
how: OOP version: `Option<Box<dyn State>>`; state methods take `self: Box<Self>` and return the next state.
`Option::take()` moves the state out so it can be replaced.
Typestate version: one struct per state; transitions consume `self` and return the next type.
Methods exist only on the states where they are valid.
Choose run-time flexibility (trait objects) or compile-time guarantees (types).

idea: **Patterns** describe the shape of a value, and they appear in many more places than `match`. A `let` statement is a pattern: `let (x, y) = point;` destructures a tuple. Function parameters are patterns: `fn print(&(x, y): &(i32, i32))`. So are the targets of `for` loops (`for (i, item) in list.iter().enumerate()`), `if let`, `while let`, let-else, and closure parameters. Learning patterns once pays off everywhere.

Patterns come in two kinds. An **irrefutable** pattern matches any possible value of its type: `x`, `(a, b)` for a pair, `Point { x, y }`. A **refutable** pattern can fail to match: `Some(x)` does not match `None`, and `1..=5` does not match 9. Where a pattern appears decides which kind is allowed. `let`, function parameters and `for` loops require irrefutable patterns, because there is no sensible thing to do if they fail. `if let`, `while let`, let-else and `match` arms accept refutable ones, because they say what happens on failure.

The compiler enforces this: `let Some(x) = maybe;` alone is an error (use `if let` or let-else), and `if let x = 5` is a warning, because the condition is always true. Match arms are refutable patterns, except that the last arm often uses an irrefutable catch-all to make the match exhaustive.
how: Patterns appear in `let`, parameters, `for`, `if let`, `while let`, let-else, `match`, closures.
Irrefutable: always match (`x`, `(a, b)`, struct destructuring).
Refutable: may fail (`Some(x)`, literals, ranges).
`let`/parameters/`for` need irrefutable; `if let`/`while let`/let-else/`match` handle refutable.
Use let-else to bind a refutable pattern for the rest of a scope.
